text: LOGISTIC REGRESSION
A deep walkthrough of the math: from the sigmoid function to gradient descent
Why Not Just Use Linear Regression?

Classification problems ask a yes/no question: will this email be spam, will this tumor be malignant, will this customer churn? The output we want is a probability between 0 and 1 — but a straight line has no such limit.
Linear regression first computes a weighted sum of the inputs:

This score z can range from -∞ to +∞. Feeding it directly into a threshold works poorly: outliers shift the line, and nothing stops predictions from exceeding 1 or dropping below 0 — nonsensical for a probability. Logistic regression keeps this linear score, but squashes it through a function that always outputs a valid probability.
The Core Idea
Compute a linear combination z of the features, same as linear regression.
Pass z through the sigmoid function to compress it into (0, 1).
Interpret the result as P(y = 1 | x) — the probability of the positive class.
Classify by comparing that probability to a threshold, typically 0.5.
The Sigmoid Function

The sigmoid (or logistic) function maps any real number z into the open interval (0, 1). As z grows large and positive, e⁻ᶻ shrinks toward 0, so σ(z) approaches 1. As z becomes very negative, e⁻ᶻ explodes, pulling σ(z) toward 0. At z = 0, the function passes through exactly 0.5 — the natural decision midpoint.
A useful property — its own derivative:
This self-referential derivative is exactly why the gradient computation later on turns out so clean.
The Hypothesis Function & Log-Odds
Combining the linear score with the sigmoid gives the full model:
h_θ(x) is interpreted directly as an estimated probability: h_θ(x) = P(y = 1 | x; θ). It answers “given these features and the current parameters, how likely is the positive class?”
Reading it in reverse: the log-odds (logit)

This is the algebraic inverse of the sigmoid. It says logistic regression is really just linear regression on the log-odds of the outcome: θᵀx directly measures how much the evidence favors class 1 over class 0 on a log scale. A one-unit increase in a feature xⱼ shifts the log-odds by exactly θⱼ, holding everything else fixed — which is how coefficients in logistic regression are typically interpreted.
The Decision Boundary
To turn a probability into a hard label, pick a threshold — usually 0.5:

Because σ(z) ≥ 0.5 exactly when z ≥ 0, this threshold on the probability translates back into a condition on the raw linear score: predict class 1 whenever θᵀx ≥ 0. Geometrically, the equation θᵀx = 0 defines a hyperplane in feature space — a straight line in 2D, a flat plane in 3D. Everything on one side is classified as 1, everything on the other side as 0.

This is why plain logistic regression is a linear classifier: the boundary it draws is always straight, even though the probability surface curves smoothly through it. Non-linear boundaries require engineered features (e.g. x² terms) or a non-linear model.
Measuring Error: Why Not Squared Error?

Linear regression trains by minimizing squared error. Plugging the sigmoid into that same squared-error formula produces a cost surface that is non-convex — full of local minima — because the sigmoid's curvature breaks the nice bowl shape gradient descent relies on. Instead, logistic regression uses a cost built from the log function, one branch for each true label:
When the true label is 1:
When the true label is 0:

The intuition: if y = 1 but the model predicts h_θ(x) close to 0, -log(h_θ(x)) shoots toward infinity — a severe penalty for confident wrong answers. If the prediction is close to 1, the cost approaches 0 — almost no penalty for confident correct answers. The mirror-image branch handles y = 0. This asymmetric, steep penalty for confidently wrong predictions is what keeps the cost surface convex.
The Full Cost Function
This cost falls out naturally from maximum likelihood estimation. Treating each label as a Bernoulli outcome with probability h_θ(x), the likelihood of the entire training set is:

Maximizing this product directly is numerically awkward (many probabilities multiplied together underflow to 0), so we instead maximize its logarithm — and flip the sign to turn “maximize likelihood” into “minimize cost,” averaged over m examples. That gives the log loss, also called binary cross-entropy:
Because this J(θ) is convex in θ, gradient-based optimization is guaranteed to find the global minimum.
Optimizing with Gradient Descent

There's no closed-form solution for θ the way there is in linear regression, so parameters are learned iteratively. Differentiating J(θ) with respect to each parameter θⱼ — using the chain rule together with σ'(z) = σ(z)(1-σ(z)) from earlier — produces a remarkably clean result:

Every log and exponential term cancels out, leaving the same form as linear regression's gradient: the average, over all examples, of the prediction error (h_θ(x) - y) scaled by the feature value xⱼ. Each parameter then takes a small step against this gradient:
α is the learning rate, controlling step size. All θⱼ are updated simultaneously, each iteration nudging predictions closer to the true labels until J(θ) converges to its minimum.
Putting It All Together
A linear score θᵀx is squashed by the sigmoid into a valid probability P(y=1|x).
That probability is thresholded at 0.5 to draw a linear decision boundary in feature space.
Parameters are fit by maximizing likelihood, equivalent to minimizing convex log loss.
Gradient descent updates each θⱼ using the same clean form as linear regression: error × feature.
